text: Your child can likely count to 20 or beyond and may start understanding simple addition. Use real objects — "You have 3 grapes, I'll give you 2 more" — to make math tangible.
Writing letters and their name with growing control is a big accomplishment. Offer lined paper and celebrate progress rather than perfection.
Your child is developing empathy and can recognize when others are sad or upset. Talk about feelings in books and real life to strengthen this skill.
Skipping, climbing confidently, and throwing a ball overhand show that gross motor skills are well-developed. Keep offering varied physical challenges.
Your child may start to understand the concept of time — today, tomorrow, yesterday. A simple calendar can help them grasp days, weeks, and upcoming events.
Your child can follow multi-step instructions and remember rules. Give them small responsibilities like setting the table to build confidence.
Friendships are becoming more stable and meaningful. Your child may have a best friend and start navigating conflicts more independently.
Your child may start sounding out simple words or recognizing sight words. Reading together nightly remains the single best literacy activity.
Your child can draw recognizable pictures with details like houses with windows and people with fingers. These drawings reflect how they understand their world.
Attention span is growing — your child can focus on a single activity for 10-15 minutes. Provide opportunities for sustained focus without interruption.
Your child may start comparing themselves to peers. Emphasize effort over outcome and celebrate individual strengths to build healthy self-esteem.
Rhyming, clapping syllables, and identifying beginning sounds are pre-reading skills developing now. Play word games to reinforce them naturally.
Your child is learning to take turns in conversation — listening, then responding. Model this by giving them your full attention when they speak.
Problem-solving becomes more sophisticated. When your child faces a challenge, guide them through thinking of solutions rather than solving it for them.
Your child can understand and tell simple jokes. Humor is a complex cognitive skill that involves surprise, wordplay, and social awareness.
Your child needs 10-13 hours of sleep per 24 hours. Most children this age have dropped naps, but some 4-year-olds may still need one. Protect bedtime even on busy days.
A winding-down period of 30 minutes before bed — reading, quiet talk, gentle stretching — helps your child's brain shift from active to sleep mode.
If your child is starting school, consistent sleep becomes even more critical. Tired children have difficulty concentrating, learning, and managing emotions.
Nightmares may still happen and often involve themes from daily life. Talk about the dream briefly, offer comfort, and help them feel safe.
Your child can start taking ownership of parts of their bedtime routine — choosing pajamas, brushing teeth, picking a book. Independence builds cooperation.
If your child resists bedtime because they want more time with you, try building in 10 minutes of special one-on-one time before the routine starts.
Keep the bedroom cool, dark, and quiet. Your child may want to help arrange their room for sleep — choosing where the nightlight goes or how pillows are placed.
Avoid screens for at least one hour before bedtime. The stimulation and blue light make it harder for your child's brain to prepare for sleep.
If your child wakes early and can't fall back asleep, teach them to look at books quietly in bed until it's time to get up.
Big life transitions — starting school, a new sibling, or moving — can temporarily disrupt sleep. Extra comfort and routine consistency help them adjust.
A gratitude practice at bedtime — naming three things they're thankful for — can help your child fall asleep with a positive mindset.
If your child snores regularly or pauses breathing during sleep, mention it to your pediatrician. It could indicate sleep apnea, which is treatable.
Weekend bedtimes shouldn't differ by more than an hour from weeknights. Large shifts in schedule make Monday mornings much harder.
Physical activity during the day significantly improves sleep quality. Even on rainy days, find ways for your child to move — dancing, indoor obstacle courses, or yoga.
Your child can use a knife and fork together with increasing skill. Let them practice cutting soft foods like bananas or pancakes at meals.
If your child is starting school, involve them in packing their lunch. Children eat better when they've helped choose and prepare their food.
Teach your child about food groups in simple terms — "grow foods" (protein), "go foods" (carbs), "glow foods" (fruits and vegetables) — to build nutrition awareness.
Your child needs about 1,200-1,600 calories per day. Portion sizes should be roughly a quarter to a third of adult servings.
Picky eating often improves around age 5 as children become more willing to try new foods. Continue offering variety without pressure.
Your child can help with real cooking tasks — measuring ingredients, cracking eggs, mixing batter. These skills build math concepts and independence.
If your child eats lunch at school, talk about what they ate and what they liked. This keeps you connected to their nutrition and builds conversation skills.
Iron needs remain important at this age. Lean meats, beans, spinach, and iron-fortified cereals help prevent deficiency, which can affect energy and focus.
Peer influence on eating starts now. Your child may want to try foods they see friends eating — use this as an opportunity to introduce new things.
Teach your child to drink water when thirsty rather than reaching for juice or flavored drinks. Good hydration habits formed now last a lifetime.
Family meals together — even 3-4 times a week — are linked to better nutrition, stronger vocabulary, and closer family relationships.
Talk about food positively. Avoid labeling foods as "good" or "bad" — instead, explain that some foods are for everyday eating and some are for special occasions.
Your child can start understanding food safety basics like washing produce, not eating food that fell on the floor outside, and checking with adults about unfamiliar foods.
If your child is a slow eater, allow adequate time at meals without rushing them. Pressuring them to eat faster can create anxiety around mealtimes.
Protein at breakfast — eggs, yogurt, nut butter on toast — helps your child stay focused and energized through the morning, especially on school days.
A well-child visit during this stage is important. Your pediatrician will check vision, hearing, growth, and developmental readiness, and can provide any documentation needed for school entry.
If your child wears glasses, make sure they actually wear them consistently. Children adapt quickly and their vision development depends on proper correction.
Your child may start losing baby teeth soon. Explain that this is a normal and exciting part of growing up to ease any worry.
Hand washing before meals, after bathroom use, and after playing outside is a habit that dramatically reduces illness. Make sure your child does it consistently.
If your child has anxiety about starting school or new activities, validate their feelings and practice the new situation through role play or visiting beforehand.
Check with your pediatrician to make sure your child's immunizations are up to date. Some vaccines may be required before starting school.
Head lice can spread in school settings. Check your child's hair weekly, especially behind the ears and at the nape of the neck.
Establish a daily flossing routine. Your child's teeth are likely close together now, and flossing prevents cavities between teeth.
Encourage your child to tell you when something hurts or doesn't feel right. At this age, they can start describing symptoms, which helps you respond appropriately.
Warts are common in school-age children and are caused by a virus. They're harmless but can be treated if they bother your child.
If your child frequently complains of headaches or squints at books and screens, schedule an eye exam. Vision needs can change rapidly at this age.
Physical activity protects your child's mental health as well as their body. Active children show lower rates of anxiety and better emotional regulation.
Teach your child basic hygiene independence — covering coughs, washing hands, using tissues. These skills help them stay healthy in group settings.
Board games with simple strategy — like memory, dominoes, or checkers — build critical thinking, patience, and good sportsmanship.
Your child may be ready to learn to ride a bicycle without training wheels. Start on a flat, soft surface and let them build confidence at their own pace.
Encourage your child to create their own stories — drawn, dictated, or written. Storytelling develops literacy, creativity, and emotional processing.
Group sports or movement classes can introduce teamwork and physical fitness. Focus on fun and participation rather than competition at this age.
Building elaborate structures with blocks, boxes, or construction sets teaches engineering concepts, planning, and persistence.
Your child may enjoy simple cooking projects. Making a smoothie, assembling a sandwich, or decorating cookies combines math, reading, and fine motor skills.
Nature exploration — collecting rocks, identifying birds, or examining insects — nurtures curiosity and scientific thinking.
Musical instruments or rhythm activities develop coordination, math skills, and self-expression. Even a simple drum or xylophone offers rich learning.
Obstacle courses that include crawling, jumping, balancing, and throwing challenge multiple physical skills and can be set up with household items.
Role play with themes like doctor, teacher, or firefighter helps your child process real-world experiences and practice social scenarios.
Letter and number games — hopscotch with letters, counting jumping jacks — make early academics physical and fun.
Give your child a magnifying glass and let them explore the backyard up close. Observation skills developed through play translate to science and reading readiness.
Encourage your child to play with children of different ages. Younger kids help them practice leadership; older kids challenge them to grow.
Free, unstructured play remains essential even as scheduled activities increase. Protect daily time for your child to play however they choose.
Your child should know their full name, your phone number, and their home address. Practice regularly until they can recite all three from memory.
Teach pedestrian safety: stop at every curb, look left-right-left, and walk (don't run) across streets. Practice together on every outing.
Your child should remain in a car seat or booster until they're at least {{4 feet 9 inches|145 cm}} tall, which is typically not until age 8-12.
Teach your child the difference between a secret and a surprise. Secrets that make them feel uncomfortable should always be told to a trusted adult.
If your child walks to school or a bus stop, walk the route together multiple times. Identify safe spots and practice what to do if they feel unsafe.
Helmets are non-negotiable for biking, skating, and scootering. Your child should see you wearing one too — modeling matters more than rules.
Begin simple internet safety conversations. Even if they're not online alone, teach that personal information is private and screens are used in shared spaces.
Teach your child what to do in an emergency: call emergency services, state their name and address, and stay on the line. Practice with a play phone.
Your child can learn basic fire safety — stop, drop, and roll; stay low in smoke; meet at the family meeting point. Practice your home escape plan twice a year.
When visiting other homes, teach your child to ask before touching things or going into unfamiliar rooms. This builds respect and keeps them safe.
Ensure your child understands that no adult should ask them to keep a secret from their parents. Open communication is the best protection.
Review playground rules: no pushing, wait your turn, and tell an adult if someone is being unsafe. Your child can start self-advocating in these situations.
If your child plays outside independently, set clear boundaries for how far they can go and check in regularly. Gradually expand independence as they demonstrate responsibility.
Keep an updated photo of your child on your phone. In the unlikely event they get lost in a crowd, a current photo helps others help you find them quickly.
